hints: Start from the atomic numbers, P is 15, S is 16, Cl is 17, and write the outer $3s^2 3p^x$ part to find x for each element.
Remember that electrons fill separate 3p orbitals singly first, so think when pairing starts and how that changes the unpaired count.
walkthrough:
Count the 3p electrons**
Think of building up from Na. The $3s$ fills with 2 electrons, then the $3p$ starts. P is the third element in the p block, so $3p^3$. S adds one more to give $3p^4$. Cl adds another to give $3p^5$.

Apply Hund's rule for unpaired electrons**
Picture three empty 3p boxes. P puts one electron in each box, so 3 unpaired. S must pair up one box, leaving 2 unpaired. Cl pairs a second box, leaving only 1 unpaired.

Final answer: Number of electrons in 3p subshell: P = 3, S = 4, Cl = 5.
Total number of unpaired electrons: P = 3, S = 2, Cl = 1.

hints: Recall that first ionisation always starts from one mole of gaseous atoms and removes one electron to form a 1+ ion.
walkthrough:
Build the ionisation equation**
First ionisation means removing the first, most loosely held electron. Start with gaseous P atoms, $\text{P(g)}$, and show loss of one electron to give $\text{P}^{+}\text{(g)}$ plus $\text{e}^{-}$. State symbols must both be (g).
Final answer: $\text{P(g)} \rightarrow \text{P}^{+}\text{(g)} + \text{e}^{-}$

hints: Look at the general rise from P (1060) to Cl (1260) and decide whether S should be slightly above P or clearly below P.
Compare nuclear charge across P to S to Cl and think how that alone would affect attraction for the outer electron.
Focus on the electron arrangement in S, where the fourth 3p electron must share an orbital, and what repulsion that creates.
Combine both effects to explain why S is lower than both P and Cl, not between them.
walkthrough:
Spot the anomaly**
Across a period you expect ionisation energy to rise because protons are added. But S is famous for dipping below P. That tells you the correct choice must be the lowest value, $1000\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$, below P at 1060.

Compare S with Cl**
Cl has more protons (17) than S (16) with the electron removed from the same shell and with similar shielding. Greater nuclear charge pulls the outer electrons tighter, so Cl holds its electron more strongly. That is why S is lower than Cl.

Compare S with P**
S does have one more proton than P, so you might expect S to be higher. But look at the orbitals. P is $3p^3$ with three unpaired electrons in separate orbitals. S is $3p^4$, so two electrons must share one orbital.

Explain the effect of pairing**
Two negative electrons in the same small orbital repel each other. This spin-pair repulsion outweighs the extra proton, making the paired electron in S easier to remove. So S drops below P as well.

Final answer: Correct value: $1000\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
S has the lowest first ionisation energy, with less nuclear attraction for outer electrons than P or Cl.
Cl has greater nuclear charge than S, so stronger attraction.
S has greater nuclear charge than P but has two electrons paired in one 3p orbital, so spin-pair repulsion makes the electron easier to remove.

hints: Count the total electrons in $\text{P}^{3-}$ by adding 3 to the 15 of phosphorus, then fill shells in order to $1s$, $2s$, $2p$, $3s$, $3p$.
walkthrough:
Add electrons then fill**
Neutral P has 15 electrons. Adding 3 gives 18 electrons, the same as argon. Fill in order: $1s^2$, then $2s^2 2p^6$, then $3s^2 3p^6$. That full outer octet is very stable.
Final answer: $1\text{s}^{2}\ 2\text{s}^{2}\ 2\text{p}^{6}\ 3\text{s}^{2}\ 3\text{p}^{6}$

hints: Note all three ions have 18 electrons but different numbers of protons, 15, 16 and 17, and decide how pull per electron changes.
Check shielding, since all have the same electron arrangement, so focus on what happens to attraction as nuclear charge rises.
walkthrough:
Recognise an isoelectronic series**
$\text{P}^{3-}$, $\text{S}^{2-}$ and $\text{Cl}^{-}$ all have 18 electrons. The only difference is the number of protons pulling on them: 15, 16, 17.

Link protons to size**
Shielding is essentially the same because the electron shells are identical. More protons means greater effective nuclear attraction on the same outer shell, drawing it in tighter. So the largest ion is $\text{P}^{3-}$ with fewest protons, the smallest is $\text{Cl}^{-}$ with most protons.

Final answer: Ionic radius decreases from $\text{P}^{3-}$ to $\text{Cl}^{-}$.
Increasing nuclear charge with the same shielding pulls the outer electrons closer to the nucleus more strongly.

hints: Think about the reactivity order of halogens and whether bromine, being less reactive than chlorine, can displace chloride.
Recall that conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ oxidises bromides and iodides to coloured vapours but is not strong enough to oxidise chlorides.
Remember the classic test for halides with $\text{AgNO}_{3}$(aq) and the colour of each silver halide precipitate.
walkthrough:
Bromine with chloride**
A more reactive halogen displaces a less reactive one. Chlorine is above bromine, so bromine cannot take electrons from chloride. No reaction occurs, you simply see the orange brown colour of the added $\text{Br}_{2}$(aq).

Concentrated sulfuric acid with chloride**
Conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$ can oxidise $\text{Br}^{-}$ to $\text{Br}_{2}$ and $\text{I}^{-}$ to $\text{I}_{2}$, but chloride is held too strongly to be oxidised. You get steamy $\text{HCl}$ fumes which are colourless, so no visible change in solution.

Silver nitrate with chloride**
$\text{Ag}^{+}$(aq) + $\text{Cl}^{-}$(aq) gives $\text{AgCl}$(s). Silver chloride is a white precipitate, distinct from cream $\text{AgBr}$ and yellow $\text{AgI}$.

Final answer: Test 1 ($\text{Br}_{2}$(aq)): no visible reaction, solution stays orange / brown / yellow.
Test 2 (conc. $\text{H}_{2}\text{SO}_{4}$): no visible reaction, solution remains colourless.
Test 3 (dil. $\text{AgNO}_{3}$(aq)): white precipitate forms.

hints: Link the very low melting point of $1^{\circ}\text{C}$ and boiling point of $106^{\circ}\text{C}$ to the strength of forces between molecules.
Think what type of reaction with water produces misty acidic fumes, and what that tells you about the bonding.
walkthrough:
Use the melting and boiling points**
$1^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $106^{\circ}\text{C}$ are very low compared with giant lattices which melt at hundreds of degrees. That tells you $\text{POCl}_{3}$ exists as separate small molecules held together only by weak van der Waals forces that need little heat to break.

Use the reaction with water**
Fizzing with water to give misty fumes of $\text{HCl}$ and an acidic solution is hydrolysis. Covalent chlorides like $\text{PCl}_{5}$ and $\text{POCl}_{3}$ hydrolyse readily, while ionic lattices simply dissolve. Together both observations point to simple covalent.

Final answer: Relatively low melting and boiling points indicate weak intermolecular / van der Waals forces between discrete molecules.
Vigorous reaction with water to give acidic solution indicates hydrolysis, characteristic of simple covalent chlorides.

hints: Hydrolysis of $\text{POCl}_{3}$ replaces all three Cl with OH from water, giving $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$ and $\text{HCl}$, then balance water and $\text{HCl}$.
walkthrough:
Balance the hydrolysis**
Each Cl ends up as $\text{HCl}$ and the $\text{PO}$ unit ends up as phosphoric acid, $\text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4}$. You need 3 waters to supply 3 O plus H atoms: $\text{POCl}_{3} + 3\text{H}_{2}\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_{3}\text{PO}_{4} + 3\text{HCl}$. Check atoms: P 1, O 4, H 6, Cl 3 on both sides.

hints: Count outer electrons: P contributes 5, O contributes 6, each Cl contributes 7, giving 32 total, and remember P=O uses 4 shared electrons.
Plan the sharing: P shares one electron with each Cl and two with O, then add lone pairs so O and each Cl each have 8 electrons around them.
walkthrough:
Place the bonding pairs**
In the overlaps, show one dot from P and one cross from Cl for each P-Cl single bond (3 bonds total). For P=O, show two dots from P and two crosses from O in the P-O overlap to make the double bond.

Complete the lone pairs**
Give each Cl three more pairs (6 electrons) so it has 8 in total. Give O two more pairs (4 electrons) so it also has 8. P already has 5 bonds worth of electrons around it (10 electrons), which is allowed as it expands its octet. Count all dots and crosses to check 32 outer electrons.

Final answer: P shares 2 electrons with O (double bond, 4 electrons in overlap) and 1 electron with each Cl (3 single bonds).
All outer shells complete: O has 2 lone pairs, each Cl has 3 lone pairs, P has expanded octet, total 32 outer electrons shown with dots and crosses.

hints: Start with the amount, one mole of compound formed, and what the starting materials must be.
Add the precise condition for the elements, their standard states under standard conditions.
walkthrough:
State the amount and process**
Formation means making the compound from its elements, not from other compounds. You must specify one mole of compound formed.

Add the standard state condition**
The elements must be in their standard states, that is their normal physical states at $100\ \text{kPa}$ and $298\ \text{K}$, e.g. $\text{P(s)}$, $\text{O}_{2}\text{(g)}$, $\text{Cl}_{2}\text{(g)}$.
Final answer: Enthalpy change when one mole of a compound is formed from its constituent elements in their standard states.

hints: Write the enthalpy change of the reaction $2\text{PCl}_{3} + \text{O}_{2} \rightarrow 2\text{POCl}_{3}$ using $\Delta H_{r} = \Sigma \Delta H_{f}(\text{products}) - \Sigma \Delta H_{f}(\text{reactants})$.
Relate that same $\Delta H_{r}$ to bonds: breaking O=O (+496) and making two P=O bonds, then solve for $E(\text{P=O})$.
walkthrough:
Find reaction enthalpy from formation data**
Use Hess's law: $$\Delta H_{r} = 2\Delta H_{f}(\text{POCl}_{3}) - [2\Delta H_{f}(\text{PCl}_{3}) + \Delta H_{f}(\text{O}_{2})]$$ $\Delta H_{f}(\text{O}_{2}) = 0$. So $$\Delta H_{r} = 2(-592) - 2(-289) = -1184 + 578 = -606\ \text{kJ}$$ for the equation as written.

Link to P=O bond formation**
Conceptually, $\text{O}_{2}$ is split to O atoms (+496) then each O joins $\text{PCl}_{3}$ to make P=O. So $$-606 = +496 - 2E_{\text{P=O}}$$ Rearranging: $$2E_{\text{P=O}} = 496 + 606 = 1102$$ $$E_{\text{P=O}} = +551\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$ Positive because bond making is exothermic but bond energy is defined as energy required to break.
